title: Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
author: Lewis Carroll
openingText: Alice was growing very tired of sitting beside her sister on the bank with nothing to do. Once or twice she had glanced at the book her sister was reading, but there were no pictures or conversations in it. “And what use is a book,” Alice thought, “without pictures or conversations?”
about:
Alice follows a White Rabbit with a watch down a hole and arrives in a world where the rules of ordinary conversation keep turning against her. A request for directions becomes an argument about destinations; a lesson becomes an accusation; a game of croquet has equipment that refuses to stay still. Alice tries to make sense of it all with the manners, schoolwork and confidence she has brought from home. Her own changing size makes even those resources uncertain.

Published in 1865, Lewis Carroll’s short novel moves through twelve chapters of encounters, interrupted stories and recitations that go wrong. Its nonsense has precise local rules. A word can change its meaning halfway through an exchange, while a creature can remain perfectly certain that only Alice has made a mistake. The narrator shares her curiosity but also lets us see the awkwardness of her assumptions, particularly when she praises her cat to animals the cat would eat.

The tea-party, the Caterpillar and the Queen belong to the same story, but they do not offer a single lesson to decode. Carroll lets playfulness, irritation, fear and tenderness sit close together. Reading the entire book gives its familiar scenes their peculiar rhythm: Alice keeps moving, questioning and trying again, even when a conversation has led nowhere.

acclaim.quote: Few books have met with such unequivocal praise from the critics and such instantaneous favour from the public
acclaim.source: Langford Reed, Foreword to Further Nonsense Verse and Prose (D. Appleton and Company, 1926), p. 11. https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/77627/pg77627-images.html
acclaim.context: An excerpt from Reed’s retrospective appraisal of Alice’s reception, written in his own foreword. It is not presented as a review from 1865 or as a modern critical consensus.

whyItMatters.title: Conversation changes the rules around Alice
whyItMatters.body: The Hatter disputes the difference between saying what one means and meaning what one says. The Mock Turtle turns lessons into things that lessen. These exchanges make language an action: whoever controls the definition can redirect the conversation and blame the listener for the confusion. Alice sometimes catches the trick and sometimes joins it. Readers today can recognise the frustration of an argument whose terms keep changing.

whyItMatters.title: Authority depends on performances that Alice can question
whyItMatters.body: The gardeners paint white roses red to conceal a mistake, while the Queen answers difficulties with execution orders. In the courtroom, the King invents a rule and tries to turn an ambiguous poem into evidence. Carroll gives these figures the ceremonies of power without making their reasoning coherent, and Alice gradually becomes less willing to accept their conclusions. The trial remains a useful scene for thinking about how institutions treat evidence today.

whyItMatters.title: Alice’s changing body unsettles her sense of identity
whyItMatters.body: Alice measures herself against doors, tables and other creatures, but her size keeps changing before she can settle into a role. When familiar verses come out wrong, she wonders whether she has become another child. Carroll ties these questions to concrete sensations of being too large, too small, noticed or dismissed, while allowing Alice’s curiosity to persist through them. That combination can speak to present-day readers adjusting to an unfamiliar social world.

angleCards.title: Follow the words that change meaning
angleCards.text: Track the movement from tale to tail, lessons to lessen, and purpose to porpoise. Notice which misunderstandings Alice starts and which she resists.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland to follow how puns and shifting definitions shape each encounter, including the mistakes Alice makes herself.

angleCards.title: Watch Alice negotiate authority
angleCards.text: Compare the Caterpillar’s questions, the Duchess’s morals and the Queen’s commands. Attend to how Alice’s replies change as she grows more confident.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland to examine how Alice responds to people who claim the right to question, instruct or punish her.

angleCards.title: Read the poems beside the conversations
angleCards.text: Keep the recitations and songs in view. Their animals, threats and impossible situations often carry an argument forward after ordinary explanation has failed.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland to understand what the verse contributes to the humour, unease and structure of the story.

angleCards.title: Stay close to Alice’s changing scale
angleCards.text: Follow the practical consequences of each change in size: what she can reach, whom she fears and how she is identified. Notice how the narrator moves between sympathy and amusement.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland to follow the relationship between bodily scale, self-confidence and the narrator’s view of Alice.

cast.name: Alice
cast.description: A curious girl sitting beside her sister when a White Rabbit catches her attention. She talks herself through difficulties, recalls her lessons and tries to behave politely, even when the creatures she meets make that difficult.

cast.name: The White Rabbit
cast.description: A rabbit with pink eyes, a waistcoat and a watch. His anxiety about being late first draws Alice after him. His manner suggests that someone more powerful is waiting.

cast.name: The Caterpillar
cast.description: A blue caterpillar sitting on a mushroom with a hookah. His short questions leave Alice struggling to explain who she is.

cast.name: The Duchess
cast.description: A resident of a house full of pepper and noise. She is quick to judge, and just as ready to attach a moral to whatever is said.

cast.name: The Cheshire Cat
cast.description: A cat with a conspicuous grin and an unusual way of appearing. It offers Alice directions while questioning the assumptions behind her request.

cast.name: The Hatter
cast.description: A hat-seller sharing tea with the March Hare and Dormouse. He treats a conversation as an opportunity for riddles, objections and unexpected distinctions.

cast.name: The March Hare
cast.description: The Hatter’s companion, ready with an invitation or interruption. He helps maintain the tea-party’s peculiar ideas of hospitality.

cast.name: The Dormouse
cast.description: A drowsy guest between the Hatter and March Hare. Its attempts at a story must compete with sleep and the others’ questions.

cast.name: The Queen of Hearts
cast.description: A playing-card queen whose instructions leave little room for disagreement. Her court brings ceremony and constant danger into Alice’s path.

cast.name: The Gryphon
cast.description: A creature Alice meets through the Queen. It is impatient with long explanations and leads her towards another storyteller.

cast.name: The Mock Turtle
cast.description: A tearful creature with memories of schooling under the sea. His account gives familiar lessons and dances unfamiliar shapes.
